elements.element: New York law governs the Agreement.
elements.evidence: Rendered Section 10.5 retains: "This Agreement shall be governed and construed and enforced in accordance with the laws of the State of New York ... without giving effect to the principles of conflict of laws." Pre-existing language, unchanged.

elements.element: State and federal courts in New York County have exclusive jurisdiction.
elements.evidence: Added sentence: "Each Party irrevocably consents to the exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts located in New York County, New York over any dispute arising out of or relating to this Agreement." Mutual ("Each Party"), exclusive, and correctly names both state and federal courts in New York County.

elements.element: The governing law is Delaware, California, or England and Wales.
elements.evidence: The rendered clause selects New York law, not Delaware, California, or England and Wales. Not met at the fallback level, but this is immaterial because the preferred level (New York) is fully satisfied and is superior for us.

elements.element: The dispute forum is the corresponding Delaware or California courts, or the courts of London for England and Wales law.
elements.evidence: The forum added is New York County, New York, not Delaware, California, or London. Again not met at the fallback level only because the preferred forum was chosen.

elements.element: New York law governs the Agreement.
elements.evidence: Duplicate check for completeness: the New York choice-of-law sentence survives intact in the rendered text.

reasons: Both preferred elements are met in operative rendered language: New York law is retained verbatim from p0065, and a new sentence grants exclusive jurisdiction to the state and federal courts in New York County, New York. The redline is position-complete at the preferred level.

The fallback elements are unmet only because the drafter selected the higher preferred position (New York) rather than Delaware/California/England and Wales; that is not a defect and requires no repair.

Classification as a deviation is defensible: the original clause named no dispute forum at all, so it failed the forum element at both the preferred and fallback levels. A total absence of any consent-to-jurisdiction is a material gap (either party could be dragged into the Vendor's home courts), not a minor wording shortfall of the kind the playbook says to note in the rationale only.

Minimality holds. The existing choice-of-law sentence is untouched, no favourable language is deleted, and the insertion is a single sentence limited to the forum element of the checklist. No extraneous requirements (fee-shifting, jury waiver, service-of-process, injunctive-relief carve-out, forum non conveniens waiver) were smuggled in.

Intent is preserved. Nothing else in Article 10 or the commercial mechanics is contradicted; the added sentence is mutual and consistent with the New York choice of law, and there is no competing arbitration or venue clause elsewhere in the document to conflict with.

Deterministic evidence is consistent with substance: the operation applies, the governing law sits within the accepted set, and both the minimality and element-coverage gates pass on inspection of the rendered text.

Drafting nit for the drafter's awareness only (no repair required): the added sentence consents to exclusive jurisdiction but does not separately waive objections to venue or inconvenient forum. That is a preferred-position refinement, not a checklist element, so it should be noted in the rationale rather than added.
